Newly emerged alevins of the Greenback cutthroat trout measure approximately 2.25 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.25 centimeters] in total length, a diminutive size that reflects an extended period of yolk dependency before the transition to exogenous feeding. When incubated at a constant 10 °C [T = 10 °C], egg hatching typically occurs after 40 days , a value consistent with developmental rates reported for other Colorado River basin cutthroat subspecies. Following hatching, the yolk-sac larvae remain in the gravel interstitial spaces, absorbing endogenous reserves until they reach the swim-up stage. The time from fertilization to swim-up, representing the age at first exogenous feeding, is estimated at 61.5 days [ab = 61.5 days] under this same thermal regime at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. The wet weight of these newly emergent fry at the point of first feeding is approximately 0.08 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.08 grams], a modest initial mass that imposes significant constraints on early survival in the cold, high-elevation streams this subspecies inhabits.

As juveniles and sub-adults grow, the species undergoes a prolonged period of somatic development within the oligotrophic mountain streams of the South Platte and Arkansas River drainages. The ultimate total length attained by fully grown adults in these systems has been estimated at 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], although individuals in more productive habitats may approach this upper bound more readily. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of the Greenback cutthroat trout reaches approximately 150 grams [Wwi = approximately 150 grams], a value representing the maximum adult body mass recorded for the subspecies, though data quality is acknowledged as limited due to the fragmented and often marginal nature of extant populations. At the onset of sexual maturation, which typically occurs in individuals between two and three years of age sampled during the late September to October pre-spawning period, wet weight averages approximately 17 grams [Wwp = approximately 17 grams]. The total length at which puberty is attained measures 12.7 centimeters [Lp = 12.7 centimeters], a threshold that defines the transition from the immature juvenile stage to a reproductively viable organism primed for gonadal recrudescence during the subsequent spring spawning season.

First reproduction events in Greenback cutthroat trout populations of the Southern Rocky Mountains have been estimated to occur at 974 days after hatching [tR = 974 days after hatching], a value that corresponds to approximately two to three growing seasons given the abbreviated annual active period in high-elevation streams at a mean water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This delayed onset of reproductive activity is typical of salmonids inhabiting cold, resource-limited environments, where the seasonal window for successful gamete development is constrained by thermal conditions and prey availability. A gravid female during her first spawning event produces a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with fecundity per reproductive event ranging from as few as 95 eggs per clutch to as many as 281 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 95 eggs per clutch to as many as 281 eggs per clutch] under favorable resource conditions. This annual reproductive strategy is well adapted to the variable and often severe environmental conditions characteristic of the species' historic range.

Maximum lifespan estimates for the Greenback cutthroat trout in its native cold-water habitat at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] are calculated at approximately 4,076.5 days [am = approximately 4,076.5 days], equivalent to about 11 years of age under natural stream conditions where growth is slow and annual mortality pressure from piscivorous predators and angling is comparatively low. The age at which the yolk-sac larva emerges via chorion rupture, defined precisely as the hatching event, is tightly linked to local thermal conditions; at the experimental temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], successful eclosion occurs 40 days  following fertilization, a duration that shortens considerably under warmer regimes but lengthens in the colder incubation temperatures typical of snowmelt-fed redds. This relatively long incubation period reflects the energetically efficient developmental strategy of a species adapted to short growing seasons, where the yolk-sac larva stage allows continued morphological transformation without reliance on scarce early-spring prey resources. Morphometric data indicate that at the moment of egg hatching, the prolarva measures little more than a centimeter in total length, but the species' life-history strategy depends critically on the timing of this emergence relative to peak spring food availability.

Comparative life-history data for the Greenback cutthroat trout reveal a species that, despite its modest ultimate total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], exhibits remarkable longevity and delayed maturation as adaptations to extreme environmental stochasticity. The wet weight at birth of 0.08 grams [Wwb = 0.08 grams] contrasts sharply with the approximately 17 grams [Wwp = approximately 17 grams] wet weight at puberty, representing more than a 200-fold increase in somatic mass prior to the onset of reproductive effort. Analyses of scale annuli and otolith microchemistry from historical populations have validated the estimate of a maximum longevity of approximately 4,076.5 days [am = approximately 4,076.5 days] in the wild, with individuals in captive hatchery settings occasionally exceeding this duration under controlled thermal regimes at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The subspecies' sensitivity to elevated water temperatures is reflected in its reproductive timing, as first spawning at 974 days after hatching [tR = 974 days after hatching] occurs only when spring temperatures surpass the threshold necessary for vitellogenesis completion at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. Conservation efforts focusing on habitat connectivity and thermal refugia are thus paramount for preserving the remaining populations of Oncorhynchus clarkii stomias within its rapidly warming high-elevation stream network.
